## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Joash and Jehoash are two spellings of the same name. Guzik calls this a long reign that was mostly blessed: Joash advanced God's cause even though his commitment was never complete. [EW]
- Gill notes that forty years matches the reigns of David and Solomon. He places Beersheba in Simeon's territory, in the far south, and says the name Zibiah is the same as Tabitha/Dorcas (Acts 9:36). [Gill]
- Henry points out that since Joash was killed at about 47, he could naturally have reigned much longer. [MH]

**v. 2**
- Guzik, Gill and Clarke read the verse as limiting Joash's goodness to Jehoiada's lifetime. They point to 2 Chronicles 24, which says he turned to idolatry after the priest died. Clarke adds that Joash seems to have shared in the murder of Zechariah. [EW] [Gill] [Clarke]
- Henry sees it as a blessing for a young ruler to have good counsel and the wisdom to accept it. [MH]
- Trapp compares Joash to Nero, who behaved well only while Seneca guided him. [Trapp]
- Precept Austin notes that "in the sight of the LORD" means God's verdict, not public opinion. [PA]
- Bible Hub's sermon page lists a Spurgeon sermon on this verse, "A Lean-To Religion." The excerpt shown pictures Joash's goodness vanishing like morning dew once Jehoiada died, though I couldn't confirm which author wrote that passage. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_kings/12-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik calls this a half-way reform: Joash avoided the harder job of removing the high places. He quotes Poole, who says even stronger earlier kings couldn't remove them, so Jehoiada's failure is not surprising. [EW]
- Gill says the high places broke the law requiring sacrifice only at the place God chose (Deut 12). People loved them for their age and supposed holiness, and no king dared remove them until Hezekiah. [Gill]
- Henry thinks these altars were probably to the true God but competed with the temple altar. He suggests Jehoiada may have tolerated them, or that the reformers lacked the zeal or courage to act. [MH]
- Clarke says there could be no thorough reform while they stood; tolerated idolatry left a seed that later grew back. [Clarke]

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik and Gill name three income streams: the half-shekel census tax (Exod 30), money from vows by personal assessment (Lev 27), and freewill gifts. [EW] [Gill]
- Gill and Henry say "acquaintance" or "constituency" means the priests collected in their own home districts. Ryrie, quoted on Precept Austin, takes the word to mean assessors who valued the offerings. [Gill] [MH] [PA]
- Henry, Gill and Guzik say the temple was damaged partly by age but chiefly by Athaliah's sons (2 Chr 24:7). They suggest Joash cared about it because it had sheltered him as a child. [MH] [Gill] [EW]
- The Pulpit Commentary is surprised Jehoiada hadn't repaired the temple during the king's childhood. It treats the order mainly as a call for voluntary contributions. [Pulpit]

**v. 6**
Commentators suggest different causes for the delay:
- Clarke, quoted by Guzik: the priests were negligent and used the income for themselves. [EW]
- Gill: either the people were slow to pay, or the priests kept the money, or both. [Gill]
- Henry: either the priests were careless or the people didn't trust them. He adds that the priests may have needed the money to live on. [MH]
- Pulpit: the people distrusted the priests. [Pulpit]
- Chuck Smith says flatly that the priests were "pocketing" the money. [SL12]

**v. 7**
- Henry praises the king for rebuking even his old tutor. [MH]
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees: the king consulted the high priest and gave no rebuke. It adds that the verse shows no work was going on in year 23, not that none had ever been done. [Pulpit]
- Trapp says it is surprising that Jehoiada needed prodding, but notes he was very old by then. [Trapp]
- Gill takes the order to mean the king suspected the priests of keeping the money. [Gill]

**v. 8**
- Henry: the priests honestly admitted they weren't fit for the work and stepped aside. [MH]
- Gill: they willingly gave up both jobs, especially since they were under suspicion. [Gill]
- Precept Austin cites a NET note suggesting the priests held back because they wanted skilled workers to do the repairs, not themselves. [PA]

**v. 9**
- Gill: the chest stopped fraud, or suspicion of fraud, because money couldn't come out without the lid being removed. [Gill]
- Henry: money dropped in could not be taken back, a picture of the fact that what is given to God shouldn't be reclaimed. He mentions, without endorsing it, a view linking the chest's right-hand position to "let not thy left hand know…" [MH]
- Pulpit lists three benefits: protection against misuse, less temptation for needy priests, and convenience for givers. [Pulpit]
- Guzik: even willing givers need to be given an opportunity. [EW]
- Coffman calls this the first collection box in the Bible and sees the same practice still in use when the widow gave her mites (Mark 12:42). [SL12]
- McGee notes that "Joash's chest" is still used by organisations to raise money today. [SL11]
- 2 Chronicles 24:8 puts the chest outside at the gate rather than by the altar. Clarke says it was moved there later for convenience; Gill reports Lightfoot's similar view. [Clarke] [Gill]

**v. 10**
- Clarke and Gill: the king's scribe came with the high priest so that a civil official shared the oversight and no one person could be suspected. [Clarke] [Gill]
- Pulpit: the scribe's presence amounted to publishing the accounts rather than a formal audit. [Pulpit]
- Benson: the bags were probably sealed and the counting was done daily. [SL11]
- Keil & Delitzsch: the chest kept repair money separate from the priests' income, and people gave more for a clearly stated purpose. [SL11]

**vv. 11–12**
- Ellicott notes that the Hebrew verbs show the payments were made repeatedly, each time the chest was emptied. [SL11] [BH-12] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/12-12.htm
- Gill: the overseers were laymen, not priests. [Gill]
- Henry: the work should go to people whose trade it is. [MH]
- Pulpit: the temple had stood about 136 years with no recorded repairs, so all kinds of work turned out to be needed. [Pulpit]

**vv. 13–14**
- 2 Chronicles 24:14 says vessels *were* made. Gill, Henry, the Pulpit Commentary and Patterson & Austel (quoted by Guzik) all resolve this the same way: the repairs were paid for first, and the leftover money was used for vessels afterward. [Gill] [MH] [Pulpit] [EW]
- Ellicott translates "there *used* not to be made." [BH13]
- The Geneva note says the remaining money went to the king, who had the vessels made later. [BH13]
- Henry's lesson: pay for what is needed first, before ornament. [MH]

**v. 15**
- Guzik: the project had stalled from poor money management, not lack of money. [EW]
- Gill: the overseers were so plainly honest that nobody examined their accounts. [Gill]
- Henry: anyone handling public or church money should deal faithfully, knowing God will audit them. [MH]
- The Biblical Illustrator sees this honesty as evidence of how deep the reform went. [SL11]

**v. 16**
- Guzik and Henry: the repairs were not funded at the priests' expense. Henry's line is "let not the servants of the temple be starved." [EW] [MH]
- Pulpit grounds the priests' right to this money in Numbers 5:10. [Pulpit]
- Gill: this was money sent for offerings, and the surplus belonged to the priests. [Gill]

**v. 17**
- Clarke and Gill: Gath had been held by Judah since David took it. [Clarke] [Gill]
- Gill and Guzik: after Jehoiada died and Joash fell away, God used Syria as a rod of judgment (2 Chr 24:23–24). [Gill] [EW]

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Joash gave away earlier blessings instead of trusting God. He found trust hard in a crisis because he had stopped trusting in easier times. [EW]
- Gill calls the payment mean and impious, the fruit of his apostasy. [Gill]
- Henry: if paying was lawful, better to lose the gold than the temple. But Joash shamed himself, made his kingdom poorer, and invited Hazael back, which happened the next year. [MH]

**v. 19**
- Guzik: there is no record that Joash repented. He quotes Clarke: "how few of the few… continue unto the end!" [EW]
- Gill: some of the "rest of the acts" are preserved in 2 Chronicles 24. [Gill]

**vv. 20–21**
- Gill and Henry, following Chronicles: the conspirators acted to avenge Zechariah, not to seize the throne, since Amaziah succeeded peacefully. Henry says the killers were wrong to take vengeance, yet God was righteous in allowing it. [Gill] [MH]
- Wiseman, quoted by Guzik, offers another motive: discontent after the defeat by Hazael. [EW]
- Clarke: Millo was a royal building from David's time, and Silla was probably the road leading to it. Chronicles names the killers Zabad and Jehozabad, sons of an Ammonite and a Moabite woman. [Clarke]
- Gill and the Pulpit Commentary: Joash was buried in the City of David but not in the royal tombs (2 Chr 24:25). [Gill] [Pulpit]

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no source that explicitly sets denominations against each other on this chapter. What I can show is the range of emphasis among writers from different traditions:
- Gill (Baptist), Clarke (Methodist), Henry (Presbyterian/Nonconformist) and Guzik (Enduring Word) all treat Joash as someone who **fell away**. Henry says he "began in the spirit and ended in the flesh." Clarke laments how few who begin with God continue to the end. [MH] [Clarke] [EW]
- Whether this bears on Reformed versus Wesleyan views of perseverance is not discussed in anything I read.
- On v. 7, Henry (a rebuke) and the Pulpit Commentary (a consultation, no rebuke) genuinely disagree. That is a disagreement between commentators, not between denominations. [MH] [Pulpit]

## 3. Other views

- **Translation of v. 2:** The Pulpit Commentary reads "all his days *wherein* Jehoiada instructed him," noting the Septuagint, Vulgate, Luther and others take it that way. The ESV and NRSV read "all his days, *because* Jehoiada instructed him," which could mean he was good his whole life. The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) follows the first reading. [Pulpit] https://biblehub.com/2_kings/12-2.htm
- **Kings versus Chronicles:** Precept Austin, quoting Duguid, Dillard and Pratt, contrasts the two accounts. Chronicles splits the reign into good years and bad years. Kings shows the chest set by the altar; Chronicles places it at the gate, which Pratt reads as a compromise between king and priests. [PA] [PA-2Ch]
- **NET notes:** Only indirectly, via Precept Austin: the suggestion about the priests wanting skilled workers (v. 8), and the NET wording for v. 7. [PA]
- **Not covered:** I couldn't reach Bible Odyssey, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or any denominational site. So there are no Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or popular-teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace) readings in these notes.
